doc.title: Alan Raph interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: Breaking into studio work and juggling commitments
summary: Raph moved into studio work through Elgart and Mulligan, doing rock and roll and jazz dates. He explains juggling Birdland and a Broadway show, and the subterfuge he used to cover conflicts.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: You found your way into the studio scene in New York?

Yeah. I always had that in the back of my mind that I wanted to do studio work. And Mulligan, well the Elgart band was a good entree into that, and Mulligan was a very good entree into that. I started doing — through another connection I started doing a lot of the rock & roll dates. And I got fairly busy doing those things. I was doing a Broadway show and I was playing Mulligan at Birdland and I was also doing dates during the day. And I started doing some jazz dates. We did a Cy Coleman date because our bass player at the © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

time, Bill Takas was Cy’s bass player and he contracted. So we did some Sauter- Finnegan things, we did Manny Albam, we did a number of the jazz writers. It was kind of a “get me the Mulligan band” these guys are good, let’s get as many of them as we can on this date and we know we have some good guys. I was — at that point I was juggling. And juggling is the name of — that’s the story of my life was juggling. Keeping Mulligan happy when I had to send a sub to the first set at Birdland every night because I was playing a Broadway show. I was doing “A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum” which let out at eleven. And Mulligan started at Birdland at nine or nine-thirty. So Benny Powell used to sub for me. And I came in and did the second and did the night. I’d finish at four o’clock and then go home and get up early and do a couple of dates and do a show and do that again. It was kind of interesting. But juggling. Keeping one contact while you make another, and then honoring the commitments. If you overbook, and you do this all the time, you book something that’s right on the tail of something else and then you have the problem of trying to get out of the first thing a little bit early or come to the second thing a little bit late. And there’s generally a way. I mean I only once or twice had to resort to outright subterfuge. Most of the time I could lie my way.

I remember once breaking — my daughter at the time, my 43-year-old, had a little plastic cow and I broke its foot off and put iodine on it. In the middle of a rehearsal I reached in and said, “oh man, I just broke my tooth.” I managed to get out of rehearsal. I left the trombone on the chair, just to make it look really good, and I went out, took my other trombone and went and did a brass quintet date Uptown. Every now and then I’d have to do something like that but not too often.
But I have told a few lies in my day.
Have to be a little creative.
